rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and test a substantial temperature increase to probe selectivity in the crowded central cluster. The current elution window leaves ample room for subsequent gradient adjustments.

Test an intermediate temperature to seek a selectivity window between the central-cluster overlap at 40 C and the earlier overlap at 60 C. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect.

At 55 C, the temperature-sensitive central pair may separate further, while a shallower gradient should help resolve the approaching earlier pair. Increasing tG to 14 minutes should still keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test a slightly steeper gradient at the promising 55 C setting to shift selectivity in the remaining marginal pair. The earlier pair has some resolution margin, and shortening the gradient will also reduce the last-peak time.

Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF; now shorten the gradient one step to test whether full resolution can be retained with faster elution. Keep injection 5 as the benchmark if either critical pair falls below 1.5.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to alter selectivity and slightly reduce gradient slope at the shorter duration. This probes whether the earlier critical pair can recover full resolution without sacrificing the later marginal pair.

The faster gradients at 55 C compromise an earlier pair, so explore a substantially lower temperature for a different selectivity window. Injection 5 remains the maximum-score benchmark while this run tests an alternative route to faster full resolution.

Test whether a substantially steeper gradient at 60 C moves the nearly coeluting earlier pair through an elution-order reversal into useful separation. This explores a much faster alternative while retaining injection 5 as the proven maximum-score method.

Return near the fully resolved method and narrow the organic window. The shallower slope should protect the earlier critical pair, while the higher starting organic fraction may improve the later marginal pair and offset some added retention.

Lower the endpoint one grid step to recover the small resolution deficit in injection 10 through a shallower gradient. The later critical pair has some margin, and the last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Explore a faster high-temperature branch using a higher starting organic fraction to shift the earlier pair beyond its observed crossover. The eight-minute gradient may provide more spacing in the central cluster than the six-minute trial.

Test whether a shallower gradient at 60 C restores the earlier critical pair while retaining the stronger separation of the later pair. The projected last-peak time remains below 10 minutes, offering another potential maximum-score method with more resolution margin.

Preserve injection 5's successful gradient slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute while shortening the programmed gradient by lowering its endpoint. All peaks previously eluted before this new gradient ends, so full resolution should be retained.

Explore the lower-temperature side of the central-cluster crossover with a slightly shallower gradient. This tests a distinct selectivity window while retaining the established CRF 1.000 methods as benchmarks.

Shorten the programmed gradient again while preserving the successful slope from injections 5 and 14. The gradient reaches its endpoint at the outlet after the established last-peak time, so this narrower window should retain full resolution and CRF 1.000.

Seek a less marginal maximum-score method by combining a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient. Prior runs suggest this combination may improve the later critical pair while preserving the earlier pair, with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope from injection 17 to improve its sole under-resolved pair, which reached R 1.25. The later critical pair has margin at R 1.75, and the last peak is expected to remain below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction improves the later critical pair enough at 50 C to enable faster full resolution. The lower temperature may protect the earliest pair, which became under-resolved at this starting composition and 60 C.

Make the gradient shallower at injection 19's promising starting composition and temperature to test whether both marginal central pairs improve. Its last peak at 5.83 minutes leaves room to increase separation while remaining below the time-penalty threshold.

Test a shallower gradient on the opposite side of the temperature-dependent central-pair crossover. This may improve the crowded cluster seen at 40 C while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes; the established maximum-score methods remain the benchmarks.

Refine injection 11 with a slightly steeper slope, intermediate between its fully resolved result and injection 10's marginal earlier pair. This should shorten elution while potentially retaining full resolution and CRF 1.000.

Test a small slope reduction from the fastest fully resolved method to improve its earlier critical pair while checking whether the later pair remains above 1.5. This refines the local resolution margin around the established maximum-score method without approaching the time penalty.

Preserve the successful gradient slope through the entire critical cluster, then hold at a lower endpoint to test a shorter programmed gradient. The isolated last peak may elute later, but its previous 7.60-minute retention leaves room before the time penalty begins.

Use the final injection to test a slope between the fastest fully resolved method and the steeper gradient that lost resolution, seeking faster elution. If the earlier critical pair falls below 1.5, retain injection 16, which achieved CRF 1.000 with the last peak at 7.60 minutes.
